vignette:
Fatima is a 51-year-old divorced woman of Lebanese descent who works as a social ministry worker in a mid-sized American city. She was referred for psychological assessment following a period of increasing difficulty functioning at her job, and she arrived at the intake appointment with a careful, measured manner that seemed to cost her considerable effort to maintain.

The trauma Fatima carries dates to her childhood in her family's home, where her primary caregiver - her father - was frequently violent. The abuse was not incidental; it was patterned, deliberate, and physically severe. She recalls being cornered in rooms with no clear way out, held or struck while her body was forced into positions of submission - crouched, pinned, unable to move freely. There was rarely warning. The transition from an ordinary moment to one of acute danger was seamless, and her nervous system learned, over years, to treat the ordinary as suspect. What she remembers most viscerally is not any single incident but the architecture of those moments: the closed door, the proximity of another body, the way a room could become a trap.

Fatima immigrated to the United States in her early twenties and built a life that, for a long period, felt sufficiently distant from that history. Her marriage ended in her late thirties, and she channeled her energy into her work, supporting vulnerable families through a faith-based social services organization. For years, this felt purposeful and manageable. Then, approximately eighteen months ago, a series of staff restructuring changes at her organization placed her more frequently in one-on-one meetings with supervisors and colleagues in enclosed office spaces. Something shifted. The memories did not arrive as clear narratives - she has found, and continues to find, that she cannot put what happened to her into language in any coherent way. When she tries, the words dissolve. What comes instead is physical: her shoulders round inward, her body seems to fold into a posture she does not consciously choose, the same posture she was forced into as a child. She does not always recognize this is happening until someone points it out.

When recollection does surface more fully, it arrives with a surge of rage so intense that Fatima has described feeling temporarily unrecognizable to herself. This anger has surfaced at work on several occasions - a sharp, disproportionate response to a colleague's tone, a moment of visible aggression during a team meeting that left her shaken and ashamed afterward. She had come to believe that something in her was fundamentally dangerous, that she was a person who could not be trusted in proximity to others. At the same time, she was certain that she herself was perpetually at risk. She began scanning rooms the moment she entered them, locating exits before she located seats. In shared workspaces, she positioned herself near doors. She stopped accepting any assignment that required her to be alone with another person, which, in a social ministry context, meant declining home visits, intake interviews, and case consultations - the core functions of her role. Her supervisor had raised concerns. Colleagues had noticed her reluctance and attributed it to various things, none of them accurate.

Outside of work, Fatima had arranged her life along similar lines. She did not travel alone in elevators. She did not sit with her back to a room. She scanned the space behind her when walking, certain at times - even when she knew rationally that nothing was wrong - that someone was following her. She often reacted to ambiguous sounds or movements with a startle response she described as feeling like falling off a ledge. She had come to believe that her body had simply never learned the difference between then and now, that some part of her remained permanently in that childhood home, waiting.

What finally brought Fatima to seek help was a formal performance review in which her supervisor noted that her avoidance of client contact had become untenable. She had not wanted to acknowledge that her work - the one domain she had always protected - was being affected. What she is most afraid of is being seen as broken or unstable, particularly by the communities she serves. What she is most hoping for, though she expressed this quietly and with evident uncertainty, is to find a way to be in a room with another person without her body insisting it is already too late.
